authorization: User requested all 89 whole practice questions from Further Work with Functions 1A: Reciprocal and Absolute Value Graphs; teaching content excluded.
method: Ordinary promotion in isolated staging, verified once and published through a checked transaction.

classification.difficultyReason: Direct recognition using the taught reciprocal rules: identify the original zero, preserve signs and reciprocate the y-intercept. No nontrivial connection or unsignposted insight is required.

questions.mappingNote: The whole question assesses recognition of a reciprocal-function graph. Absolute-value transformations, reciprocal trigonometry and graph addition/subtraction are not assessed.
questions.methodNote: The worked answer correctly follows the supplied graphical method: exclude the original zero, retain signs, reciprocate the ordinate at x=0, and establish signed one-sided limits and end behaviour. All coordinates and limits remain exact.

classification.difficultyReason: Direct application of taught reciprocal rules to recognise the correct graph from its vertical asymptote and positive branches. No unsignposted connection or substantial linked procedure is essential.

questions.mappingNote: The assessed task is recognising the reciprocal graph. The given quadratic is supporting information; polynomial graphing is not separately assessed.
questions.methodNote: The worked solution follows the taught graphical method: exclude the original zero, preserve ordinate signs, reciprocate limiting behaviour and retain points with ordinate 1. The original approaches zero from above on both sides of x=1/2, so the supplied teaching qualification about signed approaches introduces no uncertainty here.

classification.difficultyReason: Selecting the graph requires direct application of the taught reciprocal rules: locate the original zero and preserve the signs on either side. No nontrivial connection or unsignposted insight is essential.

questions.mappingNote: The task directly assesses recognition of a reciprocal-function graph. Polynomial graphing is supporting context rather than a separately assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: The worked answer follows the supplied graphical method: exclude the original zero, preserve signs, reciprocate the fixed ordinate −1, and determine signed one-sided and end limits. Its exact coordinates and limits are retained; no alternative method is needed.

classification.difficultyReason: Requires linking reciprocal simplification to the original function's domain and explaining why an excluded input survives cancellation. This is a routine conceptual application of the taught restriction.

questions.mappingNote: The task assesses reciprocal-function domain preservation rather than interval notation. reciprocal-function-graph is the closest supplied taxonomy match; its domain restriction is explicitly taught, although this question requires an explanation rather than a sketch.
questions.methodNote: The worked answer follows the taught rule that the reciprocal exists only where the original function is defined and nonzero. It simplifies the nested reciprocal while retaining x≠−1.

classification.difficultyReason: Requires linking graphical zeros, interval signs, one-sided limits, turning points and reversed monotonicity to construct reciprocal branches. Distinguishing crossing and touching zeros is essential, but the supplied teaching explicitly develops this routine linked procedure.

questions.mappingNote: All eight parts assess graphical construction of 1/f(x). Polynomial-shaped originals provide graphical information; polynomial equation reconstruction and factorisation are not required. No absolute-value, reciprocal-trigonometric, inverse-function or graph-addition/subtraction skill is directly assessed.
questions.methodNote: The answers follow the taught graphical ordinate-reciprocation method: retain each abscissa, reciprocate nonzero ordinates, exclude original zeros, preserve signs, use signed one-sided approaches to determine divergence, reciprocate end behaviour and nonzero turning-point ordinates, and reverse monotonicity separately on zero-free intervals. Touching zeros in d and g correctly produce positive divergence from both sides. Unlabelled graphical coordinates remain approximate rather than becoming invented exact-answer requirements.

classification.difficultyReason: Requires linking graphical zeros, signs, a maximum and a nonzero horizontal limiting value to reciprocal branches and an exact range. These are routine applications of the explicitly taught reciprocal-sketching procedure.

questions.mappingNote: The whole question directly assesses reciprocal-function sketching and its resulting range. No absolute-value, reciprocal-trigonometric or sum/difference skill is assessed.
questions.methodNote: The worked answer follows taught ordinate reciprocation: exclude the original zeros, preserve signs, use signed one-sided limits for vertical asymptotes, map the maximum to a minimum and reciprocate the horizontal limiting value. It appropriately leaves graphical zero positions unlabelled rather than inventing exact coordinates.

classification.difficultyReason: The hardest essential demand is coordinating reciprocal signs, multiple vertical asymptotes, mapped turning points and one-sided limits for the cubic graphs, including the touching zero in part r. These are routine linked applications of explicitly taught rules. Neither the number of parts nor the internally reconstructed equations adds assessed difficulty.

questions.mappingNote: All eighteen parts assess sketching the reciprocal from a supplied graph. Reading polynomial features supports that task but does not independently assess polynomial graph construction. No absolute-value, reciprocal-trigonometric, inverse-function or graph-addition/subtraction skill is directly assessed.
questions.methodNote: The solutions apply the supplied graphical method: retain each abscissa, reciprocate nonzero ordinates, exclude zeros, preserve signs, use signed approaches to zero for vertical-asymptote behaviour, reciprocate end limits, and reverse monotonicity separately on sign-consistent intervals. Nonzero extrema retain their abscissae and reverse type; zero-height extrema have no reciprocal image. Parts o and p correctly use the graph's unlabelled zero positions without demanding exact surd coordinates. Parts q and r likewise retain graphical extrema without introducing an equation-finding requirement. The worked answers use signed approaches explicitly, so the separately recorded qualification issue in teaching block p5-rule-1-asymptote does not invalidate these solutions.

classification.difficultyReason: The hardest essential demand is coordinating base-function zeros, signs, turning points and reciprocal limits across several intervals, including a repeated zero. Selecting (x²−4)/2 as the base in part c is also required. These are routine linked applications of the explicitly taught reciprocal-sketching procedure; neither the number of parts nor the cubic algebra warrants Mastery.

questions.mappingNote: All eight parts directly assess sketching a reciprocal from an appropriate base function. Polynomial factorisation and base-graph recognition support that task and do not warrant secondary classifications. No absolute-value, reciprocal-trigonometric, graph-addition/subtraction or explicit domain-and-range task is present. The existing primary skill is retained; its inconsistent Mastery band and score 25 are replaced by the reviewed Development rating.
questions.methodNote: Every worked answer follows the supplied graphical method: sketch a polynomial base, exclude its zeros, preserve signs and abscissae, reciprocate nonzero ordinates, determine signed one-sided limits and end behaviour, and reverse monotonicity separately on intervals avoiding zeros. Part c correctly uses f(x)=(x²−4)/2, and part d uses f(x)=−x³. Parts f and h retain graphical turning-point mapping without imposing additional exact-coordinate calculations. Part h correctly excludes the base's zero turning point at x=−1. The supplied teaching qualification about signed approaches to zero does not obstruct these solutions: their continuous polynomial bases have the required definite signs near every zero.

classification.difficultyReason: Requires routine coordination of ordinate reciprocation, original-domain exclusions, signs, extrema and distinct one-sided and end limits. These procedures are explicitly taught; no unsignposted insight is essential.

questions.mappingNote: All four parts directly assess graphical construction of 1/f(x). Intercepts, domains, limits and extrema support that construction rather than constituting separately assessed secondary skills.
questions.methodNote: The worked answers follow the supplied teaching: retain only defined, nonzero original inputs; map ordinates to their reciprocals; preserve signs; reverse monotonicity on each signed branch; interchange nonzero maxima and minima; and reciprocate one-sided and end limits. Unlabelled graphical coordinates remain schematic, without inventing equations or exact turning-point values.

classification.difficultyReason: Requires combining domain exclusions, signed limits, turning-point reciprocation and reversed monotonicity. Part a includes distinguishing a reciprocal hole from a vertical asymptote, but the necessary reasoning follows the supplied teaching directly.

questions.mappingNote: Both parts directly assess constructing a reciprocal graph from graphical information. Domain, signs and limits support this construction; no separate secondary skill is directly assessed.
questions.methodNote: Both solutions use graphical ordinate reciprocation, preserve original exclusions, determine signed one-sided limits, reciprocate turning-point ordinates and reverse monotonicity on each continuous nonzero branch. They retain qualitative sketches without requiring an invented source equation.

classification.difficultyReason: Direct application of the taught output absolute-value rule to a linear function, followed by recognising its vertex among four supplied graphs.

questions.mappingNote: The task assesses recognising y=|f(x)| from the graph of f(x). No secondary skill is directly assessed.
questions.methodNote: The worked answer correctly follows the supplied teaching: retain y=x+2 for x≥−2 and reflect its negative ordinates for x<−2 across the x-axis. This preserves the zero at −2 and produces vertex (−2,0) and y-intercept 2.

classification.difficultyReason: Direct application of the explicitly taught input absolute-value transformation to recognise a graph from four options; no additional insight or linked procedure is essential.

questions.mappingNote: The task directly assesses recognising y=f(|x|). Polynomial graphing is an incidental prerequisite, not a separately assessed secondary skill.
questions.methodNote: The worked answer correctly follows the supplied teaching: retain the original graph for x≥0, discard its negative-x portion and reflect the retained portion across the y-axis. This gives (x−1)² for x≥0 and (x+1)² for x<0.

classification.difficultyReason: Direct application of the taught input-absolute-value transformation: recognise f(|x|), retain the nonnegative-x branch and identify its reflection. No unsignposted connection or linked procedure is essential.

questions.mappingNote: The task assesses identifying y=f(|x|). Polynomial roots and symmetry support that identification but are not separately assessed skills.
questions.methodNote: The worked answer correctly follows the supplied teaching: retain the graph for x≥0, discard the original negative-x portion and reflect the retained portion in the y-axis. This removes the original zero at -2; it does not use the output transformation y=|f(x)|.

classification.difficultyReason: Both parts directly apply taught absolute-value reflection rules to a supplied graph. Preserving the near-axis gap and reflecting the labelled intercept require care but no nontrivial reframing.

questions.mappingNote: Part a assesses y=|f(x)| and part b assesses y=f(|x|), both explicitly covered by the primary skill. No additional skill is directly assessed.
questions.methodNote: The written solutions correctly teach retaining nonnegative ordinates and reflecting negative ordinates for part a, and retaining the nonnegative-x portion and reflecting it in the y-axis for part b. However, the solution code changes the retained and reflected Bézier paths instead of transforming the supplied paths directly, contrary to the supplied graphical-path teaching contract.

classification.difficultyReason: The hardest essential demand is selecting and reflecting the appropriate portions of a supplied curved graph using the explicitly taught absolute-value rules. Both transformations are direct applications; additional parts and turning points do not introduce an unsignposted connection or linked procedure.

questions.mappingNote: All twelve parts directly assess sketching either y=|f(x)| or y=f(|x|). Polynomial equations support checking some supplied graphs, but finding equations, polynomial graph construction and domain/range calculation are not separately requested or directly assessed. No secondary skill is warranted.
questions.methodNote: Every worked answer follows the supplied teaching: output absolute value retains nonnegative ordinates and reflects negative portions across the x-axis; input absolute value retains the nonnegative-x portion and reflects it across the y-axis. Fixed intercepts and reflected key points are used correctly. The g–j solutions transform the supplied Bézier paths directly, including their control points, without assigning unsupported polynomial equations or exact turning-point coordinates.

classification.difficultyReason: Both parts directly apply a taught absolute-value reflection rule to a supplied graph. Neither requires an unsignposted connection or linked procedure.

questions.mappingNote: Both output and input absolute-value transformations are explicitly assessed. Asymptote tracking supports these sketches; no separate reciprocal, inverse or sum/difference skill is assessed.
questions.methodNote: Part a correctly instructs retaining nonnegative ordinates and reflecting negative ordinates across the x-axis. Part b correctly instructs retaining the nonnegative-x portion and reflecting it across the y-axis. However, both solution diagrams redraw the retained/reflected paths rather than consistently transforming the supplied endpoints and control points, contrary to the supplied teaching contract.

classification.difficultyReason: Requires reversing the input absolute-value transformation, identifying the original quadratic's roots and determining its coefficient from a labelled point. These are routine linked procedures.

questions.mappingNote: The requested result is a quadratic equation reconstructed from graphical information, so polynomial-equation reconstruction is primary. Understanding which half survives f(|x|) is directly assessed and warrants the secondary skill.
questions.methodNote: Uses the taught rule that f(|x|) retains f(x) for nonnegative x. The supplied worked method then uses the retained roots 0 and 4 to write f(x)=ax(x-4), and substitutes (2,-2). No unsupported turning-point coordinates are introduced.
questions.sourceContextException: The requested result is a quadratic equation reconstructed from graphical information, so polynomial-equation reconstruction is primary. Understanding which half survives f(|x|) is directly assessed and warrants the secondary skill. This directly assessed polynomial task is retained as an explicit exception to the booklet functions taxonomy branch.

classification.difficultyReason: The student recognises that the x≥0 half of the graph is f, then finds the quadratic from its roots plus one point (the y-intercept or the vertex). This is one reframing step and routine algebra, close to the 36-rated p24-q08 but with two parts.

questions.mappingNote: graph-absolute-value-of-function is the primary skill recorded on this master question; its audit-v2 review is current for this content.

classification.difficultyReason: Links a scaffolded rational rearrangement to retaining and reflecting a branch, while tracking mirrored poles, branch signs and a cusp. No unsignposted insight is required.

questions.mappingNote: The main assessment is constructing f(|x|). The translated reciprocal expression supports that construction; the question does not directly assess graphing 1/f(x) from a supplied function, so reciprocal-function-graph is not added.
questions.methodNote: Part a splits x+1 into (x-1)+2. Part b follows the taught input absolute-value rule: retain the nonnegative-x portion of 1+2/(x-1), excluding its pole, and reflect it in the y-axis.

classification.difficultyReason: Requires a scaffolded rational rearrangement followed by a routine input absolute-value transformation, with linked intercept and limiting-behaviour checks.

questions.mappingNote: Constructing f(|x|) is the assessed graph skill. Rational rearrangement is supporting algebra, and domain and range are not requested as a separate assessment.
questions.methodNote: Part a writes x-1=(x+1)-2. Part b retains the nonnegative-x branch of 1-2/(x+1) and reflects it in the y-axis, exactly following the supplied input absolute-value teaching. The original pole at x=-1 lies in the discarded portion.

classification.difficultyReason: The student does a short algebraic split, then sketches a translated reciprocal under |x| with both asymptotes, the central cusp and the sign pattern. It is a routine linked procedure, a little heavier than p24-q10 because of the asymptotes.

questions.mappingNote: graph-absolute-value-of-function is the primary skill recorded on this master question; its audit-v2 review is current for this content.

classification.difficultyReason: The hardest essential demand is selecting an appropriate preliminary function, distinguishing input from output absolute value, and linking sign intervals or symmetry with intercepts and asymptotes. These are routine linked procedures for a prepared student; the algebraic identities in e and i require no decisive unsignposted insight.

questions.mappingNote: All ten parts directly assess absolute-value graph transformations. Preliminary polynomial and reciprocal sketches support those transformations rather than independently assessing additional taxonomy skills. No graph addition or subtraction is required.
questions.methodNote: Parts a–d and f correctly retain nonnegative ordinates and reflect negative ordinates across the x-axis. Part e uses the valid identity 1/|x|=|1/x| for x≠0 to apply the same taught rule. Parts g–j retain the nonnegative-x portion of an appropriate preliminary function and reflect it across the y-axis; i correctly uses |x³|=|x|³. These methods match the supplied teaching and preserve the necessary domain exclusions. Every supplied TikZ curve formula and plotting interval was checked against these transformations.

classification.difficultyReason: The hardest essential demand is coordinating reciprocal branch signs, touching and crossing zeros, one-sided limits, turning points and end behaviour on a supplied graph. These are routine linked applications of explicitly taught rules. The two absolute-value transformations directly assess distinguishing input reflection from output reflection.

questions.mappingNote: Part a assesses reciprocal graph construction and supplies the most advanced demand. Parts b and c directly assess both absolute-value graph transformations, warranting the secondary skill. No polynomial equation, root multiplicity calculation, graph addition or subtraction is assessed.
questions.methodNote: Part a follows the taught point mapping (a,b) to (a,1/b), excluding undefined inputs and zeros, preserving signs and ordinates ±1, determining one-sided asymptote directions, reciprocating nonzero turning-point heights and reversing monotonicity. Part b retains nonnegative portions and reflects negative portions in the x-axis. Part c retains the nonnegative-x portion and reflects it in the y-axis. These methods preserve the graphical nature of the supplied function without inventing an equation or exact unlabelled extrema.

classification.difficultyReason: The hardest essential demand is combining reciprocal domain exclusions, three branch signs, one-sided limits, transformed turning points and a nonzero horizontal limit in one sketch. These are routine linked applications of the supplied teaching; neither absolute-value transformation requires an unsignposted insight.

questions.mappingNote: Part a directly assesses reciprocal graph construction and has the most advanced assessed demand. Parts b and c directly assess output and input absolute-value transformations, warranting the secondary skill. No graph addition or subtraction is assessed.
questions.methodNote: Part a follows the taught graphical method: retain abscissae, reciprocate nonzero ordinates, exclude zeros, preserve signs, reverse monotonicity and determine asymptotic behaviour from limits. Part b retains nonnegative portions and reflects only negative portions in the x-axis. Part c retains the nonnegative-x portion and reflects it in the y-axis. No algebraic equation is invented for the graphically defined function.

classification.difficultyReason: The hardest essential demand is coordinating reciprocal domain exclusions, one-sided limits and asymptotes for a discontinuous graphical function. These are routine linked applications of the supplied teaching; the absolute-value transformations also follow explicitly taught rules.

questions.mappingNote: Part a directly assesses reciprocal graph construction and carries the greatest demand. Parts b and c directly assess both output and input absolute-value transformations, justifying the secondary skill. No graph addition or subtraction is assessed.
questions.methodNote: Part a uses ordinate reciprocation, preserves signs and fixed ordinates ±1, excludes undefined inputs and zeros, and derives branch behaviour from one-sided and end limits. Part b retains nonnegative ordinates and reflects negative ordinates across the x-axis. Part c retains nonnegative inputs and reflects their graph across the y-axis, determining the domain from where f(|x|) is defined. These methods match the supplied teaching without inventing an equation.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply |f| to a cubic and an exponential with a horizontal asymptote that reflects to y=4. These are direct single transformations, with the exponential the harder part.

questions.mappingNote: graph-absolute-value-of-function is the primary skill recorded on this master question; its audit-v2 review is current for this content.

classification.difficultyReason: The hardest essential demand is coordinating signs, one-sided limits, end behaviour and turning-point reciprocation to construct three reciprocal branches. These are routine linked procedures for a prepared student.

questions.mappingNote: Part b directly assesses reciprocal-function graphing and supplies the primary skill. Part a explicitly assesses polynomial graphing using roots and the vertex, so graph-polynomials-factored is directly assessed as a secondary skill.
questions.methodNote: The solutions follow the supplied teaching: sketch the original parabola, exclude its zeros from the reciprocal domain, preserve signs, reciprocate its turning-point ordinate, determine signed one-sided limits and end behaviour, and reverse monotonicity separately on each permitted interval. Factoring and completing the square support part a without replacing the taught reciprocal approach.
questions.sourceContextException: Part b directly assesses reciprocal-function graphing and supplies the primary skill. Part a explicitly assesses polynomial graphing using roots and the vertex, so graph-polynomials-factored is directly assessed as a secondary skill. This directly assessed polynomial task is retained as an explicit exception to the booklet functions taxonomy branch.

existingTransferReview.note: Decision 2 (James, 11 November 2026): published on the recorded review covering each question's current content; no new model review.

bankProjection.note: Source-confirmed category headings are omitted only from bank prompts and presentation. Explicit equivalent fraction notation repairs satisfy bank validation. Source booklet content and all questions are retained.
